title: How To Have A Nicer, Friendlier Class
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes the common frustration of realizing a class simply isn't very nice, either to the teacher or to each other, and critiques the two typical teacher responses: demanding civility through lectures and threats, or overwhelming students with unconditional kindness and second chances. Both approaches fail, he argues — the first breeds resentment and rebellion, while the second causes students to lose respect and view the teacher as a pushover. His proposed solution is to combine both qualities simultaneously: a kind, easygoing disposition paired with faithful, unwavering accountability. This combination communicates that disrespect won't be tolerated, but that consequences are never personal, and that forgiveness is always extended the next day. Linsin admits some mystery remains about exactly why this recipe works so well, promising a future article to unpack it further, but insists confidently that any teacher, regardless of how challenging their current class seems, can transform it this way.
points: Demanding civility through lectures and threats alone tends to increase resentment and behind-the-back rebellion.
Overwhelming students with unconditional kindness alone causes them to lose respect for the teacher.
Combining gentle, easygoing warmth with unwavering commitment to accountability is the key to a nicer, more civil class.
Consequences delivered under this combined approach are never personal, and forgiveness is extended fresh each day.
Any class, regardless of how difficult it currently seems, can be transformed using this combined strategy.
quotes: Teachers tend to respond in one of two ways. Either they get angry and demand civility through lectures, threats, talking-tos, and how-dare-yous. Or they overwhelm their students with kindness.
The first will cause your students to dislike you. It will cause behind-the-back rebelliousness and resentment. It will bring tension into your classroom and cause more incivility, not less.
The problem with the second approach is that your students won’t respect you. They’ll view you as a pushover. You’ll be brushed aside, if not run over.
To improve the civility in your classroom, you must combine a kind, easygoing disposition with a faithful and unwavering commitment to accountability.
This sends the message that while rudeness and disrespect toward you or their fellow classmates won’t be tolerated, even a sliver, it isn’t personal.
